lede: A camera, a projector and a magnifying glass all use the same converging lens. The only thing that changes between them is how far the object sits from the lens. One construction, drawn three times, gives you all three.
can: Draw the axis, the lens, F and 2F on both sides before any ray
Construct the standard rays and mark the image where they cross
Describe any image with the same three words, in the same order

md: Hold a magnifying glass close to this page and the letters grow. Move it slowly away and they blur, then flip upside down and shrink. Nothing about the lens changed. The only thing that changed was how far it was from the page.

md:
Before a single ray: draw the **principal axis**, the **lens** as a vertical line with outward arrowheads, then mark **F and 2F on both sides**, equally spaced, and stand the **object** on the axis as an upright arrow.
Here the focal length is 5 cm, so F is 5 cm out and 2F is 10 cm out on each side.

prompt: In the scaffolding above, how many crosses mark focal points before any ray is drawn?
options: four: F and 2F on each side of the lens
two: F on each side of the lens
one: F on the far side only
answer: four: F and 2F on each side of the lens
explain: Four. Two of the three ray rules are defined by F, and the image's position is read against 2F, so all four go on first.

md:
All three start at the **tip** of the object and all three carry an **arrowhead**.
**Ray 1**: parallel to the axis, then **through F** on the far side.
**Ray 2**: **straight through the optical centre**, undeviated.
**Ray 3**: **through F on the near side**, then **parallel** to the axis.
Any two locate the image; the third checks them.

title: Why does the ray through the centre not bend?
md: At the very middle the two faces are parallel, so that part of the lens behaves like a thin rectangular block: the ray bends one way going in and the same amount back coming out. The sideways shift is too small to draw.

prompt: In the diagram above, a ray leaves the tip of the object travelling parallel to the principal axis. Where does it go after the lens?
options: through the principal focus on the far side
through the principal focus on the near side
straight on, parallel to the axis
answer: through the principal focus on the far side
explain: Through F on the far side. Parallel in means through F out; that is the first of the three rules.

md:
Mark the image where the rays cross, and draw it as an arrow from the axis. Then describe it with the **same three words in the same order**: **real or virtual**, **upright or inverted**, **magnified or diminished**.
Here the object is 15 cm from the lens and the image comes out 7.5 cm away, 1.0 cm tall against an object 2 cm tall: real, inverted, diminished. That is a **camera**.

prompt: In the camera diagram above the image arrow points downwards. Which of the three describing words does that fix?
options: inverted
virtual
diminished
explain: Inverted. Pointing down is what inverted means; whether it is real and whether it is smaller are two separate judgements.

md:
**Question.** An object 2 cm tall stands 7.5 cm from a lens of focal length 5 cm. Find the image.
**Step 1** — 7.5 cm is between F (5 cm) and 2F (10 cm), so this is the projector case.
**Step 2** — draw ray 1 and ray 2 from the tip; they cross on the far side.
**Step 3** — read the crossing point off the grid: 15 cm from the lens, 4 cm tall, pointing down.
**Answer** — real, inverted, magnified.

prompt: On the projector diagram above, how far from the lens is the image, in cm?
explain: 15 cm. Read it off the grid where the rays cross, and check it is beyond 2F, which is where a projector's image always is.

md:
Bring the object **closer than F** and the rays leave the lens still spreading, so they never cross. Trace them **backwards** with dashed lines and they appear to come from a point on the **same side as the object**.
With the object 3 cm from this lens the image is 7.5 cm from it on the object's side and 5 cm tall: **virtual, upright, magnified**.

prompt: In the magnifying-glass diagram above, why are the construction lines drawn dashed?
options: because no light actually travels along them
because the rays are weaker on that side of the lens
because the lens is thinner there
answer: because no light actually travels along them
explain: No light goes there. The dashed lines show where the rays appear to come from, which is exactly what makes the image virtual.

caption: One test settles it: could you catch this image on a screen?

md:
A **real** image forms where light really arrives, so you can catch it on a screen — a cinema screen, a camera sensor, a piece of card. A **virtual** image is only where the light **appears** to come from; put a screen there and nothing lands on it.
That is why a virtual image is drawn with dashed construction lines, and why the two real cases are the ones with a screen in the story.

prompt: A student holds a screen where a magnifying glass appears to form its image and sees nothing on it. What does that tell them about the image?
options: it is virtual, because no light actually reaches that place
it is real, because the screen is in the way
the lens is the wrong shape
answer: it is virtual, because no light actually reaches that place
explain: Virtual. The image is perfectly visible through the lens, but the light never gets to where it appears to be, so a screen catches nothing.

title: Two parts of this video CCEA does not examine
md: Lenses are separate-Physics content on AQA and Edexcel, so every good video on this topic is made for Triple and carries more than CCEA asks. Skip the **concave (diverging) lens ray diagrams** and the **magnification = image height ÷ object height** calculation: CCEA wants the image described in words, not as a number.

prompt: CCEA asks you to describe the image a converging lens forms. In what form should that description be given?
options: in words: real or virtual, upright or inverted, magnified or diminished
as a magnification worked out from the two heights
as the ratio of the image distance to the object distance
answer: in words: real or virtual, upright or inverted, magnified or diminished
explain: In words, three of them, in that order. The magnification calculation belongs to the separate-Physics specifications.

task: Drag the object slowly in from the far left and write down the three words at four positions: beyond 2F, at 2F, between F and 2F, and inside F. You will have built the strip in section 6 yourself, and you will see the moment the image flips.

prompt: In the simulation you drag the object inwards from far away. At which position does the image stop being real and become virtual?
options: as the object passes F
as the object passes 2F
it never becomes virtual with a converging lens
explain: At F. Outside F the rays still cross on the far side and the image is real; inside F they leave spreading, so the image is virtual and upright.

md:
Draw the axis, the lens, F and 2F on both sides and the object before any ray.
Construct the three standard rays, each with an arrowhead, from the tip of the object.
Mark the image where the rays cross and read its distance and height off the grid.
Describe any image as real or virtual, upright or inverted, magnified or diminished.
Name the camera, the projector and the magnifying glass from where the object sits.

This is a printed grid with the lens and the object already on it, and a mark for each part of the construction: one per correctly drawn ray, one for the arrowheads, one for the image in the right place. The last marks are the three describing words. If you are stuck, mark F and 2F on both sides first and draw the ray straight through the centre: it is the easiest of the three and it always helps.
